overview: Griqualand West connects an older Griqua homeland with the diamond fields around Kimberley. Britain proclaimed a territory here in 1871; it was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1880. The map’s 1878 to 1914 window therefore includes decades when this was a region within a larger colony, not a separate state. The imported outline also excludes Kimberley, although the historical territory included the town. Its history includes Griqua communities, African migrant workers and colonial settlers.

periods.title: British territory and colony
periods.summary: Diamond mining and competing land rights shaped the British administration.

periods.title: A region after annexation
periods.summary: Cape annexation ended the separate colonial administration; the imported map label persists.

items.text: Griqua communities formed through the histories of Khoisan people, people of European descent and people whose ancestors had been enslaved. The Kok and Berends families drew followers north through Namaqualand and along the Orange River. These communities existed well before Britain created a colony bearing their name.

Earlier settlements such as Klaarwater, later Griquatown, combined herding, hunting and trade; wheat was also grown around mission settlements. Horses and wagons connected households to distant markets. Missionary John Campbell described five languages being spoken at one settlement: an unusually busy place for anyone trying to follow every conversation.

Captain Nicholas Waterboer was awarded the disputed diamond fields in the 1871 arbitration. That award did not preserve independent Griqua control: British colonial rule followed. The territory’s name can otherwise make this abrupt transfer of power easy to miss.

Under the 1871 digging rules, a claim measured 30 feet by 30 feet, about nine metres on each side. Inspectors marked boundaries with pegs and kept registers. Digging for diamonds meant both moving earth and keeping up with licences, payments and paperwork.

Doctor J. W. Matthews recalled that early diggers paid as much as a shilling for a bucket of water brought from springs four miles away. Writing in 1887, he described a later company supply from the Vaal River, about twenty miles away, serving mines and private homes. Water infrastructure mattered as much to daily life as shiny stones.

Matthews’s 1873 complaint about a jail hospital described a leaking tent where patients lay on a dusty floor without beds. His later account recorded hospital expansion and an isolation ward in 1882. The contrast shows the difficult work of building healthcare in a fast-growing mining settlement.

In 2003, a storm-water trench accidentally cut into unmarked graves near Kimberley’s Gladstone Cemetery. Researchers examined 107 skeletons, thought mostly to be migrant mine workers who died between 1897 and 1900. Their study brings people often missing from grand diamond-industry stories back into view.

The Gladstone study found fractures and changes associated with heavy physical work, alongside evidence of infectious disease. Researchers interpreted these together with records of dangerous mining and crowded living conditions. Diamond wealth and a worker’s health could follow very different paths.

Matthews also described Catholic mission education in the 1880s, including a school attended by about 200 people from the Indian community. His account places migration and schooling beside the better-known mining story: Kimberley’s classrooms drew on a much wider world.

Sol Plaatje edited Tsala ea Becoana from Kimberley in the early 1910s. Its four pages carried both Setswana and English. At first, the printing press was in King William’s Town, hundreds of miles from the editorial office: getting a newspaper made involved a remarkable amount of travel for the words.

The newspaper enterprise drew support from a network including Barolong landowners at Thaba Nchu, Thomas Mapikela and the publisher John Tengo Jabavu. This was a collaboration across towns, giving African readers and writers a public forum during an era of racial exclusion.

Written language sample: “Tsala ea Becoana” means “Friend of the Bechuana,” the historical English title recorded by the archive. A surviving issue is dated 25 February 1911 and catalogued as chiefly Setswana with some English, published in Kimberley. This is a local newspaper from the later regional phase.

ending.text: Griqualand West’s separate colonial administration ended with Cape annexation in 1880, not with the map’s 1914 endpoint. Its towns and communities continued. The later hospital, cemetery and newspaper evidence belongs to that continuing regional history.
